summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to develop the flat patterns for sheet-metal and plate fabrications: cylinders, ducts, elbows, lobster-back bends, tees, cones, hoppers and transition pieces. You will plan the job, do the calculations, make the geometric constructions, find true lengths, develop patterns by the parallel line, radial line and triangulation methods, add the right allowances, make templates, and mark, form and check the finished parts while leading a small team.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **pattern development**: working out the flat shape that must be cut from sheet or plate so that, when it is rolled, folded or bent and joined, it makes the three-dimensional part on the drawing. A hood, a duct, a hopper, a tank shell, a pipe bend or a branch cannot be made accurately without it.

At Level 3 you do more than follow a method. You choose the method that suits the shape, do the calculations, allow for the thickness of the material and the type of seam, check your own and other people's work, and organise a team so the part is right first time. A mistake in a pattern is copied into every part cut from it.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other providers, and fabricators who set out ducting, hoppers, chutes, tanks and pipe fittings for workshops, factories, farms and building sites.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Read the drawing, find the sizes, thickness, seams and joints, choose the method, and plan the work, checks and roles.
Work out girths, mean sizes, true lengths, slant heights, sector angles, bend angles, polygon sizes, plate needs and masses.
Bisect lines and angles, divide lines and circles, construct polygons, tangent arcs and ellipses.
Find true lengths and true shapes
Read plan and elevation, and find the true length of sloping lines and the true shape of sloping cuts.
Use the parallel line, radial line and triangulation methods for cylinders, bends, tees, cones, pyramids and transition pieces.
Allow for thickness, seams, edges and weld preparation; make labelled, full-size templates.
Transfer patterns to sheet or plate, nest them to save material, cut, and form by rolling, folding and bending.
Check sizes, girths, diagonals and fit against the drawing, record the results and report errors.
Share out the work, set independent checks and model tests, and keep the job safe.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, choosing the method, true lengths, calculations, pipe bends and intersections, parallel line, radial line and triangulation development, allowances, constructions, templates, forming, checking, safety and supervision.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms or figures (for example stretch-out, generators, lap, bending rolls, match marks, notch, full size, sweep, or a worked length or angle) and essays in full sentences, with calculations set out.

**Practical tasks** done as a team: develop, make and inspect a square-to-round transition piece in sheet steel; and develop wrap-around templates and make an equal tee and a three-piece 90° lobster-back bend in steel pipe.

blocks.note: Most marks are lost on sizes, not on methods. Write every working down, use the mean sizes, check each answer a second way (a model, a second calculation or a measurement), and keep π as 3.142 unless you are told otherwise.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Planning the job, tools and safety

blocks.h: What you need from the drawing

ul: The **shape** and the kind of surface: cylinder, prism, cone, pyramid, transition, or a combination.
The **sizes**, and whether they are inside, outside or mean sizes. Drawings of plate work often give outside or inside diameters; patterns are worked from the **mean** (mid-thickness) sizes.
The **material** and its **thickness**.
The **seams**: where they go and what kind they are (lap, grooved, riveted, butt welded), and the **joints** to other parts (flanges, laps, branch holes).
Any **tolerances**, the quantity, and the drawing's revision letter.

head: Method
Use it for
How it works
rows: Shapes whose surface lines run parallel: cylinders, pipes, square and rectangular ducts, prisms, oblique cuts, elbows, lobster-back bends, tees and branches
The girth is laid out as a straight stretch-out line, and the length of each surface line is carried across from the elevation
Shapes whose surface lines all meet at one point (the apex): right cones, right pyramids and their frustums
The pattern is swung from the apex, with the true slant length as the radius
Shapes the other two cannot handle: transition pieces (square-to-round, rectangle-to-round), oblique cones, offset hoppers
The surface is split into triangles; the true length of every side is found and the triangles are built up in order
Girths, slant heights and sector angles are worked out with formulas and set out directly

blocks.h: Where to lay the pattern out

ul: **Full size** on paper, card or thin sheet, to make a template; or directly on the plate.
On the **workshop floor** for large hoppers and cones, using trammels and chalk lines.
In **CAD**, printed full size or sent to a CNC plasma or laser cutter. Always check key sizes on a print: printers often scale a drawing to fit the paper.

head: Tool
Use
rows: Stepping equal spaces, drawing small arcs and circles
Large arcs and circles, such as cone patterns
Scriber, soapstone, paint marker, centre punch
Marking lines and key points on metal
Long straight lines on large plates and the floor
Joining plotted points in a smooth curve
All the working; record every step

blocks.h: Planning the work as a team

flow: Brief the team with the drawing; agree the method, the seam positions and the allowances
One member works out the sizes; a second member checks them independently
Draw the pattern full size and make a paper or card model; check the model's sizes before any metal is marked
Plan the nesting of the parts on the sheets or plates available
Mark and check, cut, form, then check the finished part against the drawing
Record the results, and stop at any failed check to find and fix the cause before going on

head: Hazard
Controls
rows: Gloves for handling and cutting; deburr every edge; carry sheet on edge
Work out the mass first; use two people or lifting aids; lift with a straight back
Tidy, swept area; knee pads; regular breaks to ease back strain; keep the area marked off so people do not walk over it
Keep hands well clear of the nip; never feed a plate by hand close to the rolls; loose clothing, rags and gloves can be drawn in; know where the stop is
Guards in place; eye protection; hearing protection for grinding; clamp work
Hot work rules: screens, PPE, ventilation and an extinguisher

ul: **Circumference** (girth) = π × diameter, with π = 3.142.
**Mean diameter** = outside diameter − thickness, or inside diameter + thickness.
Example: a shell 600 mm inside diameter in 8 mm plate has a mean diameter of 608 mm, so the plate length is 3.142 × 608 ≈ 1 910.3 mm.
Working back: **diameter** = circumference ÷ π.
**Arc length** of a sector = 2 × π × radius × (angle ÷ 360).
**Chord** across an arc = 2 × radius × sin(half the angle). Dividing a circle of radius R into n equal parts gives chords of 2 × R × sin(180° ÷ n).

blocks.p: Most true lengths and slant heights come from **Pythagoras**: the long side (hypotenuse) = √(one short side² + the other short side²). For example, a line with a plan length of 240 mm that rises 180 mm has a true length of √(240² + 180²) = √90 000 = 300 mm.

ul: **Slant height** L = √(base radius² + vertical height²).
**Sector angle** of the pattern = 360° × base radius ÷ slant height.
The arc of the pattern must equal the girth of the base: a quick check on any cone pattern.

For a **frustum** (a cone with its top cut off), extend the sides to the apex. By similar triangles, the distance from the small end up to the apex = small radius × height ÷ (large radius − small radius).

head: Shape
Inside angle at each corner
Angle at the centre between corners
Useful sizes
rows: Across flats = 1.732 × side; across corners = 2 × side
Across flats = 2.414 × side; across corners = 2.613 × side

blocks.p: Inside angle = (number of sides − 2) × 180° ÷ number of sides. Centre angle = 360° ÷ number of sides. The perimeter of a hexagonal or octagonal duct is simply the number of sides × the side length, plus any lap.

ul: Steel weighs about **7.85 kg per square metre for each millimetre of thickness**. A 2 440 mm × 1 220 mm sheet has an area of about 2.98 m²: in 3 mm plate it weighs about 2.98 × 3 × 7.85 ≈ 70 kg.

For discs or blanks set out in straight rows, divide each sheet side by the part size and round **down**, then multiply. For example, 300 mm discs on a 1 220 mm × 2 440 mm sheet: 4 across × 8 along = 32 discs, before any cutting allowance.

blocks.note: Round only at the end of a calculation, and keep one decimal place on pattern sizes. Check the answer makes sense: the arc of a cone pattern can never be shorter than the girth of the cone's base, and a frustum's apex is always beyond its small end.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Constructions let you set out accurate shapes with only a straight edge, dividers and a scriber, which is often all you have on a plate.

head: Construction
How to do it
rows: Bisect a line (and draw its perpendicular)
From each end, swing arcs of the same radius (more than half the line) above and below; join the two crossing points
From the corner, swing an arc cutting both arms; from those two points swing equal arcs that cross; join the corner to the crossing
Divide a line into equal parts
Draw a second line at any angle from one end; step the number of equal spaces along it with dividers; join the last mark to the other end of the line, and draw parallels through the other marks
Step the circle's radius round the circle six times; join the points
From each corner, swing an arc of half the diagonal; where the arcs cut the sides are the octagon's corners
Set out five centre angles of 72°, or use the radius-and-arc method your instructor shows; join the points
From each end of two diameters at right angles, swing the circle's radius to cut the circle; the points are 30° apart
Find the centre of an arc
Draw two chords on the arc and bisect each; the bisectors cross at the centre
Tangent arc of radius R joining two lines
Draw a line parallel to each line, R away, on the inside; where they cross is the centre of the arc

blocks.p: An **ellipse** is the shape of a round pipe or duct cut at an angle, and of the hole where a round pipe passes through a sloping plate or roof. It has a long **major axis** and a short **minor axis** at right angles.

flow: Draw the major and minor axes at 90°, crossing at the centre
From the centre, draw two circles: one with a diameter equal to the major axis, one equal to the minor axis
Draw 12 lines through the centre, 30° apart, cutting both circles
From each point on the large circle, draw a line parallel to the minor axis; from the matching point on the small circle, draw a line parallel to the major axis
Where each pair crosses is a point on the ellipse; join the points with a flexible curve and check that all four quarters match

blocks.p: A **trammel** gives the same ellipse quickly on large work: mark half the major axis and half the minor axis from one end of a straight strip, keep the two inner marks on the two axes, and mark the point at the end of the strip as it slides round.

ul: A round duct of diameter D passing straight up through a roof that slopes at an angle to the horizontal: the hole's minor axis = D, and its major axis = D ÷ cos(roof slope). For a 150 mm duct through a roof sloping at 20°: 150 ÷ 0.940 ≈ 159.6 mm.
A pipe of diameter D cut through at an angle to its own centre line: minor axis = D, major axis = D ÷ sin(angle between the cut and the centre line).

sections.title: Views, true lengths and true shapes

blocks.p: Development drawings use **orthographic views**: the **plan** (looking down), the **elevation** (looking from the front) and the **end view**. Your instructor will show you first-angle and third-angle layouts; the symbol on the drawing tells you which is used.

blocks.h: When does a view show the true length?

ul: A line shows its **true length** only in a view that is parallel to it.
A vertical edge shows true in the elevation; a level line shows true in the plan.

A line that slopes both ways (like the corner line of a hopper or a transition piece) is **shorter than its true length in every view**. Using a plan or elevation length for it makes the pattern too small.

blocks.p: Build a right-angled triangle: one short side is the line's **plan length**, the other is the **difference in height** of its two ends (from the elevation). The sloping side is the true length. You can calculate it with Pythagoras or draw it.

flow: Draw one vertical line equal to the height between the two ends of the shape (for a transition piece, the height between its two ends)
From the foot of that line, set out each plan length along a horizontal base line
Join the top of the height line to the end of each plan length
Each sloping line is a true length; number them to match the plan and use them to build the pattern

blocks.note: Lines that lie flat on the drawing (the edges of the square end, or the chords round the circle) are already true in plan. Only lines that slope need the diagram. Label every line so you never use a plan length by mistake.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A face that slopes to every view, such as the cut end of a pipe at an angle, shows its **true shape** only in an **auxiliary view** drawn looking square onto it. A round pipe cut at an angle has an elliptical true shape; a square duct cut at an angle has a rectangular one, longer in the direction of the slope.

In the parallel line method, the surface of the part is divided by straight lines (**generators**) that run parallel to each other along its length. When the surface is unrolled, the generators stay parallel and keep their lengths, so their lengths can be carried straight across from the elevation onto a straight **stretch-out** line equal to the girth.

blocks.h: Pattern for a cylinder cut at an angle

flow: Draw the elevation, with the sloping cut, and the plan (a circle) below it
Divide the plan circle into 12 equal parts (more for large diameters) and number the points, starting where the seam will go
Project each point up into the elevation as a generator, ending at the sloping cut
Draw the stretch-out line beside the elevation, equal to the mean girth, and divide it into the same 12 spaces
Draw a line square to the stretch-out at each division, and carry each generator's length across from the elevation
Join the tops with a smooth curve; add the seam and edge allowances

blocks.note: Put the seam on the **shortest** generator: the seam weld is then short, and it is kept clear of the joint at the other end. On large diameters use 16 or 24 divisions: more points give a truer curve.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A pipe or duct bend made from straight pieces cut at angles is a **segmented** or **lobster-back** bend. Each welded joint turns the pipe through part of the total angle, and each cut face sits at half of that turn from square.

head: 90° bend with
Pieces
Turn at each joint
Cut on each joint face (from square)

ul: For any bend: turn at each joint = bend angle ÷ number of joints; cut angle = half of that.
The middle pieces have both ends cut; the two end pieces have one square end and one cut end, so each end piece is a half piece plus any straight length needed.
Lengths are measured on the **centre line** from the bend radius R: a middle piece is 2 × R × tan(cut angle) long, and the cut part of an end piece is R × tan(cut angle).

On the outside of the pipe, the **back** (outer side) of a middle piece is 2 × (R + D ÷ 2) × tan(cut angle) long and the **throat** (inner side) is 2 × (R − D ÷ 2) × tan(cut angle), where D is the outside diameter.

blocks.p: Worked example: a 90° bend with 3 joints and a centre-line radius of 300 mm. Cut angle = 90 ÷ 3 ÷ 2 = 15°. Middle piece on the centre line = 2 × 300 × tan 15° = 600 × 0.2679 ≈ 160.8 mm.

head: Branch
What the joint line looks like
How the points are found
rows: In the front view, two straight lines meeting in a V
Project from an end view of the main, as for any tee; because the diameters are equal, the points fall on two straight lines
Unequal tee (smaller branch on a larger main)
Draw an end view of the main; project each branch generator onto the main's circle in that view, then across into the front view where it meets the same generator
The same projection, worked with the branch drawn at its true angle

ul: **Branch pattern**: stretch-out equal to the branch's mean girth, divided like the branch; carry each generator's length from the front view.

**Hole in the main**: the hole is not a simple circle on the flat sheet, because it wraps round the curve of the main. Set out its positions round the main's girth (as arc lengths measured on the main's end view) and along the main (from the front view), and join them.
The line where the two surfaces meet is called the **line of intersection**.

flow: Develop the cut full size by the parallel line method, using the pipe's outside diameter for marking
Transfer it to thin sheet or card and cut it out; mark the centre lines and quarter marks (top, bottom and the two sides)
Scribe straight lines along the pipe at the quarter points, using a length of angle iron as a straight edge
Wrap the template round the pipe with its marks on the scribed lines, and its edges meeting without overlap
Scribe or mark round the template, cut, grind and check the angle

blocks.p: In the radial line method every surface line runs from the base to one point, the **apex**. When the surface is unrolled, these lines spread out like the spokes of a fan from the apex, so the pattern is drawn with a radius equal to the **true slant length**, and the base girth is stepped round the arc.

flow: Draw the elevation; find the slant height, by drawing or by L = √(r² + h²)
With trammels set to the slant height, swing an arc from a centre point (the apex)
Work out the sector angle (360° × r ÷ L), or step the base girth round the arc in small equal chords
Join the ends of the arc to the apex; add the seam allowance
Check: the arc length must equal the mean girth of the base

blocks.p: Example: a cone with a base radius of 200 mm and a height of 150 mm has a slant height of √(200² + 150²) = 250 mm and a sector angle of 360 × 200 ÷ 250 = 288°.

blocks.h: Frustum (a cone with its top cut off)

blocks.p: Extend the sloping sides in the elevation until they meet at the apex. The pattern is then two arcs from the same centre: the **outer radius** is the slant height of the whole cone, and the **inner radius** is the slant height of the small cone that was cut off. The sector angle is the same for both.

head: Worked example (mean sizes)
Working
rows: Bottom 800 mm, top 400 mm, height 300 mm
Radii 400 mm and 200 mm; difference 200 mm over 300 mm of height
200 × 300 ÷ 200 = 300 mm, so the apex is 600 mm above the bottom

blocks.note: To check a cone pattern on the plate, measure the straight distance (chord) between the two ends of the outer arc: chord = 2 × radius × sin(half the sector angle). In the example, 2 × 721.1 × sin 99.85° ≈ 1 421 mm.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: When the radial method is awkward

ul: A very flat frustum (small difference between the diameters) has its apex a long way off, too far for trammels. Use calculation and set out the arcs in short sections, or use triangulation.
An **oblique cone** (apex not over the centre of the base) has surface lines of different lengths, so it cannot be swung from one radius. Use triangulation.
A large pattern may not fit on one plate. Split it into two or more equal **segments**, each with its own seam allowance, edge preparation and match marks.
The corner edges of a right pyramid slope both ways, so find their true length: half the base diagonal (in plan) and the vertical height make the right-angled triangle.
Swing an arc of that true length; step the base sides round it as chords; join to the centre. The pattern is a fan of triangles.
A pyramid frustum (such as a square hopper) is set out the same way, with a second arc for the top.

blocks.p: Triangulation works for almost any shape. The surface is divided into triangles small enough to be treated as flat. The **true length** of every side is found, and the triangles are then laid out one after another, each sharing a side with the last, until the pattern is complete. It takes longer than the other methods, and small errors can add up, so work carefully and check with a model.

blocks.h: Square-to-round transition (ends on the same centre)

flow: Draw the plan (the square with the circle inside it, on the same centre) and the elevation showing the height between the ends
Divide the circle into 12 equal parts and number the points
Join each corner of the square to the four circle points nearest it. This makes three narrow triangles at each corner (a curved, cone-like corner) and one large flat triangle on each side
Find the plan length of each line, then its true length with a true length diagram using the height
Start the pattern at the seam, a line down the middle of one flat side, from the mid-point of the square's edge to the nearest circle point

Build the triangles in order: the half flat triangle, then the corner triangles, then the next flat triangle, and so on round the shape, using true lengths for sloping lines, the true side of the square, and the chords between circle points
Join the circle points with a smooth curve; add seam allowances; check with a card model

blocks.p: A transition from a 500 mm square to a 300 mm round, 250 mm high (mean sizes), divided into 12. Take one corner and the three circle points from the side's mid-point to 30° round:

head: Line
Plan length
True length (height 250 mm)
rows: Corner to the point level with the side's middle
Corner to the next point (30° round)
Seam line (mid-side to the nearest circle point)

blocks.note: With 12 divisions each corner is joined to **four** circle points, and the quarter points are shared by neighbouring corners. The seam goes down the middle of a flat face, where the seam line is straight and short, not along a curved corner.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: The chord between two circle points (77.6 mm in the example) is a little shorter than the arc (π × 300 ÷ 12 ≈ 78.5 mm). Twelve chords make the round end about 11 mm short in girth. On larger work use more divisions, or step the arc lengths instead of the chords.
Use mean sizes, and check the square end's diagonals on the model and on the finished piece.
A symmetrical piece can be developed as a **half pattern**, then copied or turned over for the other half.
On an **offset** transition (the round end not on the square's centre) every line has a different true length: number and find each one separately.
An **oblique cone** is triangulated between the apex and the base points: each line from the apex has its own true length.

blocks.p: When metal is bent or rolled, the outside stretches and the inside is squeezed. Between them is a line that keeps its length, the **neutral axis**. Patterns are worked on the neutral axis.

ul: **Rolled plate** (cylinders, cones): the neutral axis is taken at mid-thickness, so use the **mean** diameters and mean slant heights.

**Tight bends in sheet**: the neutral axis lies nearer the inside face. The developed length is the flat lengths plus a **bend allowance** for each bend, from a chart, the press-brake maker's figures or a test bend.
On thin sheet the difference is small; on thick plate it decides whether the part fits. Using the outside diameter of a 600 mm (outside) shell in 10 mm plate gives a plate about 31 mm too long.

head: Allowance
Typical amount (check the drawing or the shop's practice)
rows: Add the width of the lap once
Add about three times the width of the groove, shared between the two edges
Add about two and a half times the wire's diameter
Subtract the root gap from the length; prepare bevels as the WPS says
Allow for the cut width (kerf) when parts are cut next to each other

blocks.p: Cut a small **notch** at corners and at the ends of folded or wired edges, so that edges do not overlap and bunch up when the part is formed.

ul: Templates are made **full size** (1 : 1) in card, hardboard or thin sheet.
Mark every template with the job, the part number, the drawing revision, the quantity, "this side up" or the hand, the seam position, and whether allowances are included.
Add **centre lines** and quarter marks, and **match marks** where two parts must line up when assembled.
Check a new template against the drawing and a model before it is used, and store templates flat and dry.
Plan the **nesting** first: lay the patterns on the sheet so they fit closely, with seams where they are easy to weld and inspect.
Transfer the pattern with a scriber or soapstone, and light centre-punch marks at key points; check key sizes and diagonals before cutting.
Cut sheet with snips, a nibbler or a guillotine, and plate with plasma or oxy-fuel; deburr and prepare the edges.

**Bending rolls** (three rollers) form plate into cylinders and cones. Because the rolls cannot bend the very ends of a plate, **pre-bend (set)** the ends first on a press or in the rolls, or the shell will have flat spots on each side of the seam.
Roll a cone by feeding the small end more slowly than the large end, or with the rolls set at a slant, as the machine allows.
Check the curve as you go with a **sweep**: a curved template cut to the radius.
Fold sheet in a folder or press brake, or form it by hand over bench stakes with a mallet.

head: Check
How
rows: Wrap a tape round the outside and compare with π × the outside diameter
Measure the diameter at several angles
Measure each side and both diagonals: equal diagonals mean square, not twisted
Measure the height between the ends at several points
Gap and alignment even along the seam; edges prepared for welding
Offer up to the mating part, or check bolt holes against its flange; match marks lined up

head: Fault
Likely cause
rows: Cone seam edges do not meet
Sector angle too small, or the pattern was worked from inside sizes
Cylinder too big or the seam overlaps
Plate length worked from the outside diameter instead of the mean
Flat spots each side of a seam
Pattern or forming error; diagonals of the square end not checked
Chords used instead of arcs; uneven forming; too few divisions
No match marks, or the template used the wrong way up

blocks.p: Record each measurement against the drawing size and tolerance, with a pass or fail, the date and your name. If a part was wrong, the job report should say what the error was, what caused it and how it was put right, so the same mistake is not made again.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can take the information I need from a drawing and choose the right development method for a shape.
I can plan a development job, share out the work and set independent checks.
I can work with safe practice on sheet edges, heavy plate, floor layouts and bending rolls.
I can work out girths from mean sizes, and diameters from girths.
I can use Pythagoras for true lengths and slant heights, and similar triangles to find a cone's apex.
I can work out a cone's sector angle and check a pattern by its arc or chord.
I can work out polygon angles and across-flats and across-corners sizes.
I can construct bisectors, equal divisions, hexagons, octagons, tangent arcs and ellipses.
I can find true lengths with a true length diagram.
I can develop patterns by the parallel line method for oblique cuts, bends, lobster-back bends and tees.
I can work out the cut angle and piece lengths of a lobster-back bend.
I can develop cones, frustums and pyramids by the radial line method.
I can develop a square-to-round transition by triangulation.
I can add the right allowances for thickness, seams and edges, and make labelled templates.
I can nest, mark, cut and form parts, and check them against the drawing.
I can find the cause of a pattern fault and record it.

terms: Apex
The point where all the surface lines of a cone or pyramid meet
Auxiliary view
A view drawn looking square onto a sloping face, to show its true shape
Bend allowance
The length of the neutral axis through a bend, added to the flat lengths
Bending rolls
A machine with three rollers that forms plate into cylinders and cones
Development
The flat pattern that forms a 3-D part when rolled, folded or bent
Ellipse
An oval with a major and a minor axis; the shape of a round pipe cut at an angle
Frustum
A cone or pyramid with its top cut off parallel to the base
Generators
Lines drawn along the surface of a cylinder or cone to plot a development
Girth
The distance round a part; for a cylinder, π × the mean diameter
Lap
The extra strip added to a pattern so two edges can overlap and be joined
Line of intersection
The line where two surfaces meet, such as a branch and a main
Lobster-back bend
A bend made of straight pieces of pipe cut at angles and welded together
Match marks
Marks on two parts that line up when they are assembled correctly
Mean diameter
The diameter at mid-thickness: outside diameter minus the thickness
Neutral axis
The line in bent metal that keeps its length
Nesting
Laying patterns close together on a sheet to save material
Notch
A small cut-out at a corner so folded edges do not overlap
Parallel line method
Development for shapes whose surface lines are parallel
Pre-bending (setting)
Bending the ends of a plate before rolling to avoid flat spots
Radial line method
Development for shapes whose surface lines meet at an apex
Sector angle
The angle of a cone pattern: 360° × base radius ÷ slant height
Slant height
The true length from the apex of a cone to its base edge
Stretch-out
The straight line, equal to the girth, on which a parallel line pattern is drawn
Sweep
A curved template used to check the curve of rolled plate
Template
A full-size pattern used to mark out parts
Transition piece
A part that joins two different shapes, such as square to round
Triangulation
Development by dividing a surface into triangles and finding their true lengths
True length
The real length of a line, which shows only in a view parallel to it
True length diagram
A diagram that turns plan lengths and a height into true lengths

c1.title: A fan transition for a poultry house near Spaldings
c1.text: A poultry farm near Spaldings, Clarendon, needs a square-to-round transition in 1.2 mm galvanised sheet to join a 400 mm square fan housing to a 250 mm round duct. The two ends are on the same centre and 300 mm apart (all mean sizes). Javier, the team leader, has divided the round end into 12 and drawn the plan. From one corner of the square, the plan length to the circle point level with the middle of the side is 213.6 mm.

c2.title: A feed hopper in Balaclava
c2.text: A feed mill in Balaclava, St Elizabeth, has ordered a conical hopper in 6 mm plate. The drawing gives outside diameters of 1 006 mm at the top and 406 mm at the bottom, and a vertical height of 400 mm. The shop stocks 2 440 mm × 1 220 mm plates. Shauna is to develop the pattern by the radial line method.

c3.title: A lobster-back bend for a pump discharge in Bethel Town
c3.text: A pumping station near Bethel Town, Westmoreland, needs a 90° lobster-back bend in steel pipe of 168.3 mm outside diameter. The drawing asks for five pieces with four welded joints and a centre-line bend radius of 400 mm. Dwight is making wrap-around templates for the cuts.

c4.title: A kitchen extract duct in Treasure Beach
c4.text: A guest house in Treasure Beach, St Elizabeth, is having a new kitchen extract. A 200 mm round duct rises straight up through the kitchen roof, which slopes at 30° to the horizontal, and lower down it joins a 300 mm round main duct as a branch at 90°. Annette is setting out the roof sheet and the branch.

c5.title: Checking patterns at a shop in Montego Bay
c5.text: Kadeem leads a team at a sheet-metal shop in Montego Bay, St James. A pattern printed full size from the computer has a 100 mm check line that measures 97 mm. The team must also mark octagonal cover plates measuring 600 mm across the flats, and two trainees are about to lift a full 2 440 mm × 1 220 mm sheet of 6 mm plate onto the marking table.

questions.q: Why can Javier not use the 213.6 mm plan length directly in the pattern?
o: The line slopes, so the plan shows it shorter than it is
The plan was drawn at half size so it fits on the paper sheet
Plan lengths include the lap, which must come off
The line is curved, so it must be measured with string
questions.why: A line that rises between the square end and the round end is shortened in the plan. Its true length comes from a right-angled triangle made of the plan length and the 300 mm height.

questions.q: What is the true length of that line?
questions.why: True length = √(213.6² + 300²) = √(45 625 + 90 000) = √135 625 ≈ 368.3 mm. Adding the two lengths (513.6 mm) or taking their difference (86.4 mm) is wrong: they meet at a right angle.

questions.q: The seam runs down the middle of one flat face, from the middle of a square side to the nearest circle point. Its plan length is 75 mm. What is its true length?
questions.why: The seam line also rises 300 mm, so its true length is √(75² + 300²) = √95 625 ≈ 309.2 mm. It is the shortest line on the face, which is one reason the seam goes there.

questions.q: The card model's round end comes out a little small. What is the most likely cause?
o: The pattern was worked from the mean sizes of the sheet
Chords were used, and each is shorter than its arc
The seam was put down the middle of one flat face of the piece
The true length diagram used the full 300 mm height
questions.why: Each chord between circle points (about 64.7 mm here) is shorter than its arc (about 65.4 mm), so twelve of them make the round end about 9 mm short in girth. Correct by using arc lengths or more divisions.

questions.q: Which diameters should Shauna use for the pattern?
o: 1 006 mm and 406 mm, as the drawing gives
1 012 mm and 412 mm, adding the thickness
1 000 mm and 400 mm, the mean sizes
994 mm and 394 mm, the inside sizes
questions.why: Rolled plate keeps its length at mid-thickness, so the pattern uses mean diameters: outside diameter minus the 6 mm thickness, giving 1 000 mm and 400 mm.

questions.q: Using the mean sizes, how far below the bottom of the hopper is the apex of the full cone?
questions.why: The radii are 500 mm and 200 mm, a difference of 300 mm over 400 mm of height. By similar triangles the apex is 200 × 400 ÷ 300 ≈ 266.7 mm below the bottom (666.7 mm below the top).

questions.q: What is the outer radius of the hopper pattern, measured from the apex?
questions.why: The outer radius is the slant height of the whole cone: √(666.7² + 500²) = √694 444 ≈ 833.3 mm. 666.7 mm is only the vertical height of the full cone.

questions.q: Before marking, Shauna needs the angle between the two straight edges of the flat pattern. What is it?
questions.why: Sector angle = 360° × base radius ÷ slant height = 360 × 500 ÷ 833.3 ≈ 216°. The inner arc gives the same: 360 × 200 ÷ 333.3 ≈ 216°. 144° is the gap left out of the full circle.

questions.q: The pattern will not fit on one plate, so Shauna splits it into two equal segments. What sector angle does each segment have?
questions.why: Two equal segments share the 216° sector, so each is 108°. Each new edge needs its own seam allowance, edge preparation and match marks.

questions.q: Dwight's templates mark the cut on each end of the three inner sections. At what angle off square are these cuts?
questions.why: Four joints share the 90°, so each joint turns the pipe 90 ÷ 4 = 22.5°. Each cut face is half of that from square: 11.25°.

questions.q: How long is a middle piece, measured along the pipe's centre line?
questions.why: Middle piece = 2 × R × tan(cut angle) = 2 × 400 × tan 11.25° = 800 × 0.1989 ≈ 159.1 mm. 157.1 mm is the curved arc of a smooth bend, and 79.6 mm is the cut part of an end piece.

questions.q: How long is the back (outer side) of a middle piece?
questions.why: On the back the radius is R + D ÷ 2 = 400 + 84.15 = 484.15 mm, so the length is 2 × 484.15 × tan 11.25° ≈ 192.6 mm. 125.7 mm is the throat, worked with 400 − 84.15 mm.

questions.q: Why must Dwight line each wrap-around template up with lines scribed along the pipe before marking?
o: So all the cuts line up and the bend stays flat
So the template cannot slip while it is being cut out
So the pipe is easier to clamp in the vice for cutting
So the cut length can be read off the scribed lines
questions.why: The throat and back of every cut must sit on the same two lines. If one template is turned round the pipe, that piece twists the bend out of plane; scribed lines at the quarter points keep every cut lined up.

questions.q: What size is the elliptical hole in the roof sheet for the 200 mm duct?
questions.why: Across the slope the hole is the duct's diameter, 200 mm. Up the slope it is 200 ÷ cos 30° = 200 ÷ 0.866 ≈ 230.9 mm. 173.2 mm comes from multiplying by cos 30° instead of dividing.

questions.q: To set out the roof hole by the concentric circles method, what diameters should Annette's two circles be?
o: 230.9 mm and 200 mm, the two axes
300 mm and 200 mm, the two ducts
200 mm and 100 mm, the duct and its radius
questions.why: The two circles of the concentric circles method have diameters equal to the major and minor axes. Points are found where lines from matching points on the two circles cross.

questions.q: Why is the hole cut in the flat sheet of the 300 mm main not a 200 mm circle?
o: The branch must be smaller than its hole to allow for welding
It follows the main's curve, so it is longer round the girth
The hole must be an ellipse because the roof slopes at 30°
Holes in ducts are always set out oval to let air flow better
questions.why: Along the main the hole is 200 mm long, but round the main it follows the curve, so on the flat sheet it is longer (about 219 mm here). Its shape is found by projection and measured round the main's girth.

questions.q: What should Kadeem do about the printed pattern?
o: Use it, as 3 mm is close enough on a sheet-metal pattern
Add 3 mm to each size on the pattern by eye as it is marked
Use it, but cut every part a little bigger than marked
Reprint it at actual size and measure the check line again
questions.why: The 97 mm line shows the printer scaled the drawing (here to 97%), so every size is wrong. Reprint at 100% (1 : 1) and check the line and key sizes before marking.

questions.q: What length is each side of an octagon that measures 600 mm across the flats?
questions.why: Across flats = 2.414 × side, so side = 600 ÷ 2.414 ≈ 248.5 mm. Dividing by 2.613 (the across-corners factor) gives the wrong 229.6 mm.

questions.q: About how much does the full 6 mm sheet weigh?
questions.why: Area = 2.44 × 1.22 ≈ 2.98 m²; mass ≈ 2.98 × 6 × 7.85 ≈ 140 kg. That is too heavy for two people to lift safely by hand, so use lifting aids.

questions.q: When thin sheet is folded to a tight inside radius, where does its neutral axis lie?
o: On the outside face of the bend
Exactly on the inside face of the bend
Nearer the inside face than the middle
questions.why: In a tight bend the inside is squeezed hard and the neutral axis moves towards it, so bend allowances come from a chart or a test bend. For gentle rolling, as in cylinders, it is taken at mid-thickness.
